title: Build an Online Store Homepage That Opens the Right Shopping Door
summary: Build an online store homepage that features timely collections, useful categories, honest promotions, and faster paths from arrival to product.
body_markdown:
An online store homepage is not a compressed version of the entire catalog. It is the first merchandising decision a shopper encounters. The online store homepage should recognize why someone arrived, present a small number of useful entrances, and make the next choice feel easier.


That requires more than a large banner. Highlighting seasonal collections prominently gives timely demand a clear destination. Directing shoppers toward popular categories supports broad exploration. Showing promotional offers clearly protects trust, while creating faster paths to products helps decisive visitors reach an item without touring every homepage section.


## Give the opening screen four jobs


1. **Identify the store:**


State what is sold and who it is for before asking for a click.


2. **Choose a timely lead:**


Feature one collection that reflects current customer demand and available stock.


3. **Preserve a stable route:**


Keep recognizable category and search access visible when the campaign changes.


4. **Explain the offer:**


Show the benefit, qualifying conditions, deadline, and destination together.


Use those jobs to review the first phone screen and desktop viewport. The Strikingly guide to


[better online store navigation](https://www.strikingly.com/blog/posts/better-online-store-navigation-makes-shopping-feel-effortless)


treats categories, search, collections, filters, and product pages as one connected shopping system. The online store homepage should introduce that system rather than compete with it.


## Lead with a current shopping mission


*Glow Online Shopping Template from Strikingly*


A seasonal collection works best when it answers a recognizable mission: preparing for warm weather, choosing graduation gifts, refreshing a workspace, or finding travel essentials. Highlighting seasonal collections prominently means giving that mission a clear name, useful image, short promise, and direct collection link. It does not mean changing the entire brand identity for every calendar event.


Before highlighting seasonal collections prominently, confirm the included products, stock position, delivery window, pricing, geographic limits, and removal date. A campaign that leads to unavailable items makes the online store homepage feel neglected. Give one person responsibility for the collection from launch through removal.


Keep the seasonal layer distinct from the permanent catalog. Directing shoppers toward popular categories should still help people who do not share the campaign interest. The Strikingly article on a


[smarter ecommerce merchandising strategy](https://www.strikingly.com/blog/posts/turn-browsing-into-buying-with-a-smarter-ecommerce-merchandising-strategy)


recommends rotating editorial displays while preserving stable category paths.


On a small catalog, highlighting seasonal collections prominently may require only one homepage section with four to eight products. Larger stores can use a collection preview that opens a deeper page. Strikingly's guide to


[multiple store sections](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/206388882-Adding-Multiple-Store-Sections)


explains how different categories can appear in separate sections without rebuilding store settings.


Judge the lead collection by qualified product visits, not banner clicks alone. If visitors open the campaign and immediately return, the message may promise a range the destination does not deliver. Highlighting seasonal collections prominently succeeds when the collection helps a shopper narrow the catalog and continue.


## Make popular categories useful, not ceremonial


*Pawfect Food Template from Strikingly*


Directing shoppers toward popular categories gives visitors a stable map beneath the changing campaign. Select categories using demand, revenue, customer questions, strategic importance, and breadth. “Popular” should reflect evidence rather than whichever category has the most attractive photograph.


Use customer language in every category label. “Everyday Skincare” is more informative than an internal range name; “Gifts Under $50” states a constraint. The official


[Simple Store categorization guide](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/206388862-Simple-Store-Product-Categorization)


covers categories, subcategories, product tags, display options, and category-specific SEO fields.


Directing shoppers toward popular categories also requires honest visual scale. Do not give six category cards equal weight if two contain most shopper demand. Lead with the strongest routes, then provide a restrained “Shop all categories” path. An online store homepage should make priority visible without making the remainder impossible to find.


Review each route as a promise. When directing shoppers toward popular categories, the card label, image, and linked products must agree. A category called “New Arrivals” should not contain year-old stock, and a “Best Sellers” route should have defensible sales evidence. Remove labels when their basis expires.


Category routes and seasonal routes can overlap without becoming duplicates. Highlighting seasonal collections prominently may combine products from several permanent groups, while directing shoppers toward popular categories preserves the ordinary shelf system. That distinction lets the homepage respond to a moment without teaching returning customers a new navigation model every week.


## Present an offer as a complete decision


*Skin Care Template from Strikingly*


Showing promotional offers clearly means placing the benefit and its important conditions together. State whether the promotion is a percentage discount, fixed saving, free shipping, bundle price, gift, or member benefit. Include the dates, minimum spend, eligible products, region, code requirement, and exclusions that could change the decision.


Avoid an exciting headline with terms hidden elsewhere. Showing promotional offers clearly means that if a message reads “20% off selected gifts,” the destination identifies eligible gifts and displayed prices support the claim. Strikingly's


[store coupon guidance](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/900000129746-Store-Coupons-for-Returning-Customers-Members-Only-Coupons)


illustrates discounts connected to defined customer groups and campaigns.


Showing promotional offers clearly also means designing the expired state before launch. Decide whether the banner disappears, the link redirects to the permanent category, or the page explains that the offer ended. Showing promotional offers clearly protects against stale campaigns, which damage trust. The online store homepage needs an owner, start time, end time, and post-campaign destination.


Showing promotional offers clearly does not require overwhelming ordinary shopping. Use one announcement, one collection preview, and a visible destination; repeating the same offer in every section adds noise. Directing shoppers toward popular categories should remain possible for visitors seeking something outside the campaign.


Measure more than redemption. Compare product views, add-to-cart activity, order value, margin, unavailable-item clicks, and support questions. Showing promotional offers clearly should reduce questions about eligibility. Highlighting seasonal collections prominently should reveal which seasonal mission attracts serious browsing rather than accidental clicks.


## Create different shortcuts for different levels of intent


*Strikingly Mobile Checkout Page*


Creating faster paths to products begins by recognizing that shoppers arrive with different amounts of certainty. A decisive visitor may search for a model or product name. An exploring visitor may choose a category. A gift buyer may start from budget, recipient, or occasion. The online store homepage should support these routes without forcing all three through the hero campaign.


Enable


[Site Search](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/115000185121-Site-Search)


when the catalog is large enough to justify direct retrieval. Search quality depends on descriptive product names and complete copy. Creating faster paths to products fails if a customer searches “waterproof backpack” while the relevant item is described only by an internal collection name.


Use


[Product Filter](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/900002185366-Product-Filter)


inside broad categories where price or product options meaningfully narrow the choice. Directing shoppers toward popular categories gets someone to the right shelf; filters then help them choose within it. Avoid exposing controls that produce mostly empty or identical results.


Creating faster paths to products can also come from selected product previews. The


[Product Showcase guide](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/900000132726-Showcase-Your-Product)


covers product imagery, prices, categories, buttons, and detailed descriptions. Use a preview when a small set deserves context; use direct store links when extra editorial copy would slow a known-item shopper.


On mobile, count taps and backtracking. Creating faster paths to products means the search icon, leading category, campaign destination, product card, and cart remain usable with one hand. Creating faster paths to products also means avoiding a dramatic image that pushes every shopping route down several screens.


## Run the homepage like a weekly shop-floor shift


The online store homepage needs a repeatable operating routine because inventory, demand, campaigns, and customer questions change at different speeds. Review it on a phone first, then on desktop. Keep one decision log so the next update reflects evidence instead of taste.


### A six-point homepage shift check


**Season:**


Confirm that highlighting seasonal collections prominently still matches the date, weather, stock, and delivery promise.


**Categories:**


Check whether directing shoppers toward popular categories reflects current behavior and business priorities.


**Offer:**


Verify that showing promotional offers clearly includes accurate terms, prices, links, and expiry handling.


**Routes:**


Test creating faster paths to products through search, category, campaign, and direct product entry.


**Proof:**


Confirm that product information and visible


[product reviews](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/900005498806-Show-Product-Reviews)


answer the doubts that appear after discovery.


**Record:**


Note one change, its reason, owner, launch date, and success measure before publishing.


Use the store records behind the presentation. Strikingly's


[product setup guidance](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/206200901-Adding-a-Product)


covers names, descriptions, imagery, product URLs, prices, options, and inventory. Highlighting seasonal collections prominently and showing promotional offers clearly are reliable only when those underlying records are accurate.


Review behavior with


[Strikingly built-in analytics](https://support.strikingly.com/hc/en-us/articles/215752348-Using-Your-Strikingly-Built-in-Analytics)


, then compare page patterns with store orders and customer questions. Creating faster paths to products should shorten discovery without reducing product understanding. Directing shoppers toward popular categories should distribute useful attention rather than repeatedly exposing the same bestseller.


Change one online store homepage decision at a time. Test a new seasonal lead, clearer category label, more complete offer, or creating faster paths to products, then record the result. The online store homepage becomes more valuable when every visible slot has a customer purpose, owner, and truthful destination.


Start with the four opening-screen jobs. Keep highlighting seasonal collections prominently tied to real demand. Keep directing shoppers toward popular categories grounded in evidence. Keep showing promotional offers clearly with their conditions, and keep creating faster paths to products for shoppers who already know what they need. That combination turns the homepage from a crowded poster into a useful shop entrance.
